rationale: The literature confirms that facial dysmorphism is a common component of FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDFBA, OMIM #618089), with features such as high/broad forehead, broad nasal tip, and thin upper lip reported across several cohorts (Gregor et al. 2018, Jansen et al. 2019, Lee et al. 2020, Silva et al. 2022). However, the claim that each of these specific craniofacial findings is present in >60-75% of cases in Gregor et al. (2018) conflicts with the primary reports. Gregor et al. (2018) describe the facial dysmorphisms as 'minor and nonspecific' rather than a distinct recurring gestalt of high penetration. Furthermore, large comprehensive cohort evaluations (e.g., Goel et al.) report that total facial dysmorphism of any kind is observed in only 67% of affected individuals, demonstrating that individual craniofacial markers cannot each occur at >60-75% frequency across FBXO11 patients.

evidence.text: Gregor et al. (2018) delineated 20 individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants and reported developmental delay, behavioral problems (17/20), seizures (5/20), microcephaly (4/19), obesity (5/20), short stature (4/20), and cleft lip/palate or bifid uvula (3/20). The paper noted that individuals displayed minor and nonspecific dysmorphic features rather than a uniform, highly penetrant craniofacial phenotype.

evidence.text: In a systematic analysis of 21 previously unreported individuals with FBXO11 pathogenic variants, facial dysmorphism of any type was found in 67% of cases, mild intellectual disability in 86%, hypotonia in 62%, and behavioral dysregulation in 62%.

source.title: Defining FBXO11-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Clinical, Molecular and Facial Assessment of 21 Patients
source.quote: Mild intellectual disability (86%), facial dysmorphism (67%), hypotonia (62%), and behavioural dysregulation (62%) were the most prevalent features.

evidence.text: Jansen et al. (2019) assessed 24 individuals with FBXO11 variants and noted that individuals initially presented without a clearly recognizable syndromic phenotype, though reverse phenotyping highlighted common features including a thin upper lip and a broad prominent space between the paramedian peaks of the upper lip.

conflicts: While high/broad forehead, broad nasal tip, hypertelorism, and thin upper lip are recurrent dysmorphic descriptors in FBXO11 cohorts, cohort-wide facial dysmorphism is only present in 67% of patients overall (Goel et al.), contradicting the assertion that each of these individual features occurs at a 60-75% frequency.

Gregor et al. (2018) and Jansen et al. (2019) describe FBXO11-related facial dysmorphism as minor, subtle, and nonspecific, emphasizing that patients often lack an overt, easily recognizable facial gestalt from dysmorphism alone.

new_directions.question_text: What is the sensitivity and specificity of computer vision facial gestalt tools (e.g., GestaltMatcher) in discriminating FBXO11-related disorder from other F-box and neurodevelopmental syndromes?
new_directions.rationale: Because individual dysmorphic features have moderate penetration (overall dysmorphism ~67%) and are individually nonspecific, objective automated facial phenotype modeling may delineate composite sub-visual gestalt markers.

new_directions.question_text: Do truncating/haploinsufficient FBXO11 variants produce a distinct craniofacial signature compared to domain-specific missense variants?
new_directions.rationale: Studies observe phenotypic pleiotropy (including TRPS-like phenocopies and severe ocular dysgenesis) with missense alleles; systematic correlation across all published cohorts will clarify phenotypic heterogeneity.
